# THE HOLDING · A SKETCH

*A game played on the living cube, in which two positions are held against each
other until a third arrives that neither was reaching for. A sketch and not a
specification: the geometry below is checked, the rules below are not yet
played.*

## I · WHY A GAME AND NOT A READING

Jung's essay of 1916 names a third outcome to a conflict in which neither side
will yield. If the conscious position simply wins, the defeated one continues
the war underground. If the unconscious one wins, the person is swept somewhere
they never chose. His claim is that when both are held in full tension, without
either being allowed to settle the matter, the psyche produces a content that
neither contained and both are somehow in. He took the name from mathematics:
an operation joining two unlike things into one expression.

**The deck's existing operations do not do this, and it is worth saying so
plainly rather than claiming a resemblance.**

- **Counter is not it.** A card and its counter sum to the Seed. That is
  cancellation, and cancellation is one of the two ordinary resolutions Jung is
  arguing against, wearing arithmetic instead of psychology.
- **Becoming is not it.** Becoming resolves every turning mark to stillness by
  a rule, computable in advance from one card alone. Jung's third cannot be
  deduced from the positions; it can only be produced by holding them.

What the deck already has that is close is the **Silence**, which refuses to
resolve in its register and redirects instead: *descend, do not translate;
widen, then ask again, or do not; surrender, interpretation ends here.* That is
a designed refusal of both ordinary outcomes. But a Silence does not make a
third thing. It only declines to let either side stand in for one.

So the gap is real, and it is a gap a **function** cannot close. A deterministic
operation cannot perform the transcendent function, because its output is
already contained in its input. **Contested play over time can.** That is the
whole reason for a game rather than another feature.

## II · THE BOARD IS ALREADY BUILT

[The living cube](../spatial/app/luminara-cube.js) holds the deck as a turnable
three by three by three: one core that never moves, six centres that turn
without translating, twelve edges, eight corners. Twelve moves, a scramble from
a declared seed, a proven way home, and measures of drift and heat.

And the eight corners divide, as any cube's do, into **two regular tetrahedra**
of four, interlocking as the stella octangula. Checked: every edge of each
tetrahedron is the same length, and each of the four body diagonals has exactly
one endpoint in each tetrahedron.

| | |
|---|---|
| the first four | the Scar, the Bridge, the Spectrum, the Crown |
| the second four | the Twins, the Void, the Beacon, the Return |

Two hands, four corners each, joined across four diagonals. The board was
waiting.

## III · THE CONFLICT IS A DYAD; THE FIELD OF THIRDS IS ITS PLANE

This is the part the geometry gives for nothing, and it is why the sketch
exists at all.

Name a conflict as a **dyad**: a card and its counter, the two positions. That
dyad is a line through the Seed.

Every line has a **plane standing perpendicular to it**, and that plane holds
nine cards. Those nine are precisely the cards that are **neither position**:
orthogonal to the conflict, taking neither side. That is the field from which a
third may arrive, and it is derived rather than chosen.

Checked, and the result has a shape worth keeping:

- For **nine of the thirteen dyads**, the perpendicular plane excludes both
  poles entirely. A third that arrives is always a genuine third.
- For the **four corner-dyads**, the body diagonals, the plane **contains its
  own poles**. In those four conflicts no outside third exists: the resolution,
  if it comes, is one of the two positions arrived at by another road.

Those four are the deepest conflicts the deck holds, the longest lines in the
cube, one of them the trinity. That the hardest conflicts are exactly the ones
admitting no external resolution is a finding, not a flaw, and the game should
present it as one rather than forbidding those dyads.

**The Seed lies in all thirteen planes.** Silence is always among the available
thirds, in every conflict without exception.

## IV · THE RULES, AS SKETCHED

**Setting.** The cube is scrambled from a declared seed, never from fresh
chance, exactly as the Sea replays rather than casts. A dyad is named as the
conflict. Its perpendicular plane is laid out as the field of thirds.

**Two players.** Each takes one position of the dyad, and with it one
tetrahedron of corners.

**Turns alternate**, one move each, under two constraints that are the whole
game:

1. **You may not negate.** The inverse of the move just played is forbidden. No
   position may be undone by simply reversing it, which is what "neither will
   yield" means in a form a cube can enforce.
2. **You may not abandon.** A move that carries **both** positions further from
   home is forbidden. Both must be kept alive, which is what "held in full
   tension" means in a form a cube can enforce.

**The tension is the state where both positions are displaced and neither is
abandoned.** Play continues in it, which is uncomfortable by construction.

**Resolution.** The game does not end when a position comes home. It ends when
**a card from the perpendicular plane comes home**: a third that neither player
was moving toward, arriving out of a field neither occupies. That card is
reported and nothing is said about it.

**Solo play.** One player holds both positions and alternates which one they
advance, under the same two constraints. The conflict is internal, which is the
case Jung was actually writing about.

## V · WHAT IS NOT DECIDED

Named honestly, because a sketch that hid these would be a specification
pretending.

- **Whether it terminates.** The two constraints may make some scrambles
  unresolvable, or may make resolution trivial. This needs playing, not
  reasoning, and the engine can simulate it faster than hands can.
- **Whether the constraints bind.** "May not increase both displacements" might
  forbid almost nothing, or almost everything. Unmeasured.
- **Whether it is interesting.** A game can be structurally perfect and dead.
- **What a player sees.** The cube's own surface is a rite with six gates. This
  is not that, and would need its own face, as the Sea sits beside the
  Wayfinder rather than inside it.

## VI · THE LAW IT MUST NOT BREAK

A third card arriving at the end of a held tension will look like an answer,
and people will read it as one. The line to hold is the one the field module
already holds: **report the structure, never the meaning.** The game may say
which card came home and from which plane. It may not say what that means for
the player, and it must never take a question at the start, because a question
at the start plus a card at the end is a reading wearing a game's clothes.

The distinction is not pedantry. A reading is chance meeting a question. This
is skill and contest meeting a structure. They share a deck and share nothing
else, and the moment the game accepts a question it becomes a divination with
extra steps, which is precisely the thing the estate's laws exist to prevent.

## PROVENANCE

*Sketched 26 July 2026 at the architect's word, from his own observation that
the cube's corners give a Merkaba and his question of whether the game is the
reading or something else. The Jungian frame is his. The geometric findings are
checked: the two regular tetrahedra and their edge lengths, the one-to-one
split of the body diagonals across them, the nine clean dyads against the four
degenerate ones, and the Seed's presence in all thirteen planes. The rules are
unplayed and are offered as a first shape rather than a design. Nothing here is
built, nothing is catalogued, and no letter is touched.*
